Numbers & logic · 2 min read

One object can belong to two groups

Sort by shape and colour, then explore why “and” and “or” select different objects.

By Biel Sardà · Published 1 Oct 2026 · Suggest a correction

A round red button fits twice

Put all red objects in one group and all round objects in another. A red round button fits both descriptions. A blue square fits neither. There is no need to force every object into exactly one group.

A set is a collection described by a rule. Here the rules are “is red” and “is round”. The shared part contains objects that meet both rules.

Try it yourself

Choose a rule below and see which objects qualify. The labels include shape and colour, so you can follow the activity without relying on colour alone.

“Red and round” selects only objects with both properties. “Red or round” selects objects with at least one property, including objects with both. This is the inclusive meaning of “or” used in the activity.

A word can change the answer

A red square satisfies “red or round” because it is red. It does not satisfy “red and round” because it is not round. Read the connecting word before counting.

In everyday speech, “or” can sometimes mean one choice but not both. A well-written puzzle should tell you when that exclusive meaning is intended. Do not assume the two meanings are interchangeable.

Keep the rule separate from the examples

Seeing two red round objects does not prove that every red object is round. The red square is a counterexample: one object that breaks that claim.

Try inventing another object for each region: red only, round only, both and neither. Being able to produce a counterexample is often more useful than collecting more examples that happen to fit.
